connections.observation: s002 records θάνατος recurring four times; s003 shows δουλεία paired with it twice. Held together, these make visible a sustained equation: the guardians must choose death over slavery (386b: πρὸ ἥττης τε καὶ δουλείας θάνατον) and must be free men (387b: ἐλευθέρους) who fear slavery more than death (387b: δουλείαν θανάτου μᾶλλον πεφοβημένους). The reversal of the comparative—from choosing death before slavery to fearing slavery more than death—makes the same relation structurally visible from two directions.

s001 accumulates a dense field of fear-vocabulary; s013 notes that φρίκη (shivering) is feared to produce θερμότεροι (hotter) guardians. Held together, these make visible a paradox within the fear-cluster: the chill of fright (φρίκη, φρίττειν) is diagnosed as producing excessive heat (θερμότεροι) rather than coldness. The fear-of-fear vocabulary thus contains opposed thermal outcomes within a single causal sequence.

s006 lists four verbs of removal applied to poetry (ἐξαλείψομεν, διαγράφωμεν, ἀποβλητέα, ἀφαιρετέα); s010 contrasts λοιδορεῖν and ἐπαινεῖν as what poets should not and should do. Held together, these make visible that the removal-sequence operates on existing reviling speech, while the requested praising speech (ἐπαινεῖν) has not yet been composed. The sequence of deletions precedes and makes space for an absent opposite that must still be spoken and made (387c: λεκτέον τε καὶ ποιητέον).

s007 shows Ἅιδης named in prose then recurring in Homeric dialect within quotations; s008 accumulates images of insubstantial dead (ψυχή, εἴδωλον, σκιαί, νέκυες); s009 tracks downward and fluttering movement. Held together, these make visible that Hades shifts from a place named in argument (τἀν Ἅιδου, τὰ ἐν Ἅιδου) to a destination of flight (Ἄϊδόσδε βεβήκει) inhabited by squeaking, darting, insubstantial forms. The prose names a location to be argued about; the poetry enacts arrival, movement, and presence within it.

s004 shows ἀκούω recurring with the verbal adjective ἀκουστέον appearing first as both positive and negative (ἀκουστέον τε καὶ οὐκ ἀκουστέον), then comparatively (ἧττον ἀκουστέον); s005 notes the proportional inversion ὅσῳ ποιητικώτερα, τοσούτῳ ἧττον ἀκουστέον. Held together, these make visible that hearing is regulated through doubled necessity—what must and must not be heard—and that poetic intensity (ποιητικώτερα) and pleasure (ἡδέα) become grounds for prohibition rather than permission. The comparative form of necessity inverts the expected relation between poetic quality and audience access.

s011 tracks verbal adjectives of necessity (ἀκουστέον, λεκτέον, ἀποβλητέα, ἀφαιρετέα, ποιητέον); s016 shows τύπος appearing as both the type to be removed and its opposite type to be made. Held together, these make visible that the final prescription (387c: τὸν δὲ ἐναντίον τύπον τούτοις λεκτέον τε καὶ ποιητέον) requires both speaking and making the opposite type, using the only two verbal adjectives applied to positive production rather than removal. The sequence of necessities thus culminates in a double requirement—to say and to make—applied to an opposite pattern not yet present in the section.

s008 accumulates images of insubstantial dead (ψυχή, εἴδωλον, σκιαί) without φρένες; s017 shows τρίζω recurring three times in adjacent quotations (τετριγυῖα, τρίζουσαι, τετριγυῖαι). Held together, these make visible that the souls lacking mind (φρένες) are given voice through repeated squeaking—the same participle τετριγυῖα applied to both a single departing soul (387a: ψυχὴ … ᾤχετο τετριγυῖα) and to the collective shades moving like bats (387a: αἳ τετριγυῖαι ἅμʼ ᾔεσαν). The concentrated sound-form makes audible what the mindless forms do: they squeak in flight and in congregation.

s012 lists four underworld proper names (Κωκυτούς, Στύγας, ἐνέρους, ἀλίβαντας) as δεινά τε καὶ φοβερὰ ὀνόματα; s001 shows δεινός and φοβερός embedded in the sustained fear-cluster. Held together, these make visible that the names themselves are classified as fearful and terrible (δεινά, φοβερὰ), sharing the adjectives applied earlier to Hades itself (386b: δεινὰ εἶναι). The underworld names thus inherit the quality attributed to the place, condensing location into nomenclature that induces φρίκη simply by being named (387c: φρίττειν δὴ ποιεῖ).

s014 shows ἀνδρεῖος in Socrates' prose requirement for courage, then ἀνδροτής in the Homeric quotation as what the soul leaves behind; s002 tracks θάνατος recurring four times. Held together, these make visible that courage (ἀνδρεῖος) is the goal of the educational prescription, while the Homer verses present manhood (ἀνδροτῆτα) as precisely what death separates from the soul (λιποῦσʼ ἀνδροτῆτα καὶ ἥβην). The poetry quoted as impediment to courage thus narrates the loss of the cognate quality (ἀνδροτής) in the event (θάνατος) guardians must not fear.

s015 shows παῖς appearing first as the starting point of education (386a: εὐθὺς ἐκ παίδων) then paired with ἀνδράσιν (387b: παισὶ καὶ ἀνδράσιν); s003 contrasts δουλεία and ἐλευθέρους. Held together, these make visible that the educational trajectory begins from childhood (ἐκ παίδων) and culminates in free men (ἐλευθέρους εἶναι), with both children and men (παισὶ καὶ ἀνδράσιν) prohibited from hearing verses that would make them fear slavery more than is proper. The pairing of ages thus spans the formation that must produce freedom rather than susceptibility to the fear of δουλεία.

s005 notes the proportional inversion: the more poetic (ποιητικώτερα) and pleasant (ἡδέα) the verses, the less they should be heard; s010 contrasts λοιδορεῖν (reviling) with ἐπαινεῖν (praising) what is in Hades. Held together, these make visible that poetic quality and pleasure attach to reviling speech about Hades, while the requested opposite—praise of Hades—is acknowledged to be both less poetic and less pleasant (ἡδέα τοῖς πολλοῖς ἀκούειν applies only to existing Homer, not to the prescribed ἐπαινεῖν). The inversion thus requires choosing against both poetic excellence and popular pleasure in favor of an undemonstrated and presumably less compelling opposite.

s006 lists four removal verbs (ἐξαλείψομεν, διαγράφωμεν, ἀποβλητέα, ἀφαιρετέα) accumulating through 386c–387c; s016 shows the opposite τύπος must be spoken and made (λεκτέον τε καὶ ποιητέον). Held together, these make visible that the section's final sentence (387c) answers the question ἀφαιρετέα ἄρα; with ναί, then immediately commands production of the opposite type. The sustained removal-sequence thus concludes not with silence but with a generative prescription whose content remains unspecified within the section.

s009 tracks downward flight and fluttering (πταμένη, κατὰ χθονός, ποτέονται); s013 notes φρίκη making guardians θερμότεροι καὶ μαλακώτεροι. Held together, these make visible that the physical movement attributed to souls—flying, going beneath earth, darting, fluttering like bats—corresponds to a feared physical effect on guardians: becoming too hot and too soft. The poetry's images of insubstantial, fluttering departure are diagnosed as producing not parallel insubstantiality but excessive heat and softness in living hearers.

elements.context: ἐν ταῖς μάχαις αἱρήσεσθαι πρὸ ἥττης τε καὶ δουλείας θάνατον

new_signals.observation: μάχη and μάχιμος appear in close proximity at 386b and 386c: the guardians must choose death in battles (ἐν ταῖς μάχαις) and the poetry is harmful to those who will be fighters (τοῖς μέλλουσιν μαχίμοις ἔσεσθαι). The lexical pair makes the battlefield context for the required fearlessness explicit.

elements.context: οὔτε ὠφέλιμα τοῖς μέλλουσιν μαχίμοις ἔσεσθαι

new_signals.observation: The request that poets not revile Hades is grounded in a double negative: such speech is neither true (οὔτε ἀληθῆ) nor beneficial (οὔτε ὠφέλιμα). Truth and utility are paired as jointly absent from the existing poetry about Hades.

elements.context: ἡγῇ τινά ποτʼ ἂν γενέσθαι ἀνδρεῖον
τἀν Ἅιδου ἡγούμενον εἶναί τε καὶ δεινὰ εἶναι

new_signals.observation: ἡγέομαι appears twice in adjacent sentences at 386b: first as Adeimantus' belief about courage (ἡγῇ = 'do you think'), then as the hypothetical guardian's belief about Hades (ἡγούμενον εἶναί τε καὶ δεινὰ εἶναι). The same verb of judgment is applied to both the interlocutor's assessment and the guardian's feared conviction.

elements.context: οἷα αὐτοὺς ποιῆσαι ἥκιστα τὸν θάνατον δεδιέναι

new_signals.observation: Comparative and superlative adverbs accumulate: ἥκιστα (least fear death), μᾶλλον (rather praise, more fear slavery), ἧττον (less to be heard). These gradations structure the argument as a series of more/less relations rather than absolute prohibitions or commands.
